title: Book 24 — The ghosts of the suitors in Hades—Odysseus and his men go to the house of Laertes—the people of Ithaca come out to attack Odysseus, but Athena concludes a peace
paragraphs: Then Hermes of Cyllene summoned the spirits of the suitors, holding in his hand the beautiful golden wand with which he closes men's eyes in sleep or wakes them as he chooses. With this he roused the spirits and led them while they followed behind him, whimpering and gibbering. Like bats that squeal as they fly through the hollow of some great cave when one has fallen from the cluster where they hang, so the spirits whined and squealed as Hermes the healer of sorrows led them down into the dark realm of death. When they had passed the waters of Ocean and the white rock, they came to the gates of the sun and the land of dreams, and then reached the meadow of asphodel where dwell the souls and shadows of those who can work no more.
Here they found the spirit of Achilles, son of Peleus, along with those of Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax, who was the finest and most handsome man among all the Greeks after Peleus's son himself.

They gathered around the spirit of Peleus's son, and the spirit of Agamemnon joined them, grieving bitterly. Around him were also gathered the spirits of those who had died with him in Aegisthus's house, and Achilles's spirit spoke first.

"Son of Atreus," he said, "we always believed that Zeus loved you more than any other hero from beginning to end, since you commanded many brave men when we all fought together before Troy. Yet death's hand, which no mortal can escape, struck you down far too early. It would have been better for you to have fallen at Troy at the height of your glory, for the Greeks would have built a mound over your ashes, and your son would have inherited your good name. Instead, you were fated to meet a most wretched end."

"Fortunate son of Peleus," replied Agamemnon's spirit, "for dying at Troy far from Argos, while the bravest Trojans and Greeks fell around you fighting for your body. There you lay in the swirling clouds of dust, all magnificent and huge, no longer concerned with your prowess in battle. We fought the entire day, and would never have stopped if Zeus had not sent a storm to halt us. Then, when we had carried you from the battle to the ships, we laid you on your bed and cleansed your fair skin with warm water and oils. The Greeks tore their hair and wept bitterly around you. Your mother, when she heard the news, came with her immortal sea-nymphs from the ocean, and the sound of great mourning rose over the waters so that the Greeks trembled with fear. They would have fled in panic to their ships if wise old Nestor, whose counsel was always best, had not stopped them, saying, 'Hold fast, Greeks, do not flee, sons of the Achaeans. This is his mother coming from the sea with her immortal nymphs to look upon her son's body.'

"So he spoke, and the Greeks feared no more. The daughters of the old sea-god stood around you weeping bitterly and clothed you in immortal garments. The nine Muses also came and raised their sweet voices in lament, calling and answering one another. There was not a Greek who did not weep at the dirge they sang. For seventeen days and nights we mourned you, mortals and immortals alike, but on the eighteenth day we gave you to the flames. Many fat sheep and cattle we sacrificed around you. You were burned in divine clothing, with rich oils and honey, while heroes on foot and horseback clashed their armor around the pyre as you burned, with the sound of a great multitude. But when heaven's flames had done their work, we gathered your white bones at daybreak and placed them in oils and pure wine. Your mother brought us a golden urn to hold them—a gift from Dionysus and the work of Hephaestus himself. In this we placed your bleached bones mixed with those of Patroclus who had died before you, and separately we enclosed those of Antilochus, who had been closer to you than any other companion after Patroclus was gone.

"Over these the Greek army built a noble tomb on a headland jutting out over the open Hellespont, so it could be seen from far out at sea by those now living and those yet to be born. Your mother asked the gods for prizes and offered them to be competed for by the noblest of the Greeks. You must have attended the funerals of many heroes, when young men prepare themselves to compete for prizes at the death of some great chief, but you never saw such prizes as silver-footed Thetis offered in your honor, for the gods loved you well. Thus even in death your fame has not been lost, Achilles, and your name lives forever among all mankind. But as for me, what comfort did I have when my fighting days were done? For Zeus planned my destruction on my return, at the hands of Aegisthus and my wicked wife."

So they talked, and presently Hermes came up to them with the spirits of the suitors who had been killed by Odysseus. The spirits of Agamemnon and Achilles were amazed to see them and went up to them at once. Agamemnon's spirit recognized Amphimedon, son of Melaneus, who had lived in Ithaca and been his host, so he began to speak to him.

"Amphimedon," he said, "what has happened to all you fine young men—all the same age too—that brings you down here under the earth? One could not pick a finer group of men from any city. Did Poseidon raise his winds and waves against you when you were at sea, or did your enemies kill you on the mainland while you were stealing cattle or sheep, or fighting to defend their wives and city? Answer me, for I have been your guest. Don't you remember how I came to your house with Menelaus to persuade Odysseus to join us with his ships against Troy? It took us a whole month before we could resume our voyage, for we had great difficulty persuading Odysseus to come with us."

And Amphimedon's spirit answered, "Agamemnon, son of Atreus, king of men, I remember everything you have said, and I will tell you fully and accurately how our end came about. Odysseus had been gone a long time, and we were courting his wife, who would not give us a direct refusal, nor would she bring the matter to an end, for she meant to bring about our destruction. This was the trick she played on us. She set up a great loom in her room and began working on an enormous piece of fine needlework. 'My suitors,' she said, 'Odysseus is indeed dead, but do not press me to marry again immediately. Wait—for I would not want my skill in needlework to go unrecognized—until I have finished a shroud for the hero Laertes, for when death takes him. He is very wealthy, and the women of the place will gossip if he is laid out without a shroud.' This is what she said, and we agreed. Then we could see her working on her great web all day long, but at night she would unpick the stitches again by torchlight. She fooled us this way for three years without our discovering it, but as time passed and she was in her fourth year, when the months were waning and many days had passed, one of her maids who knew what she was doing told us, and we caught her undoing her work. So she had to finish it whether she wanted to or not, and when she showed us the robe she had made, after it had been washed, its splendor was like that of the sun or moon.

"Then some malicious god brought Odysseus to the upland farm where his swineherd lives. His son also came there, returning from a voyage to Pylos, and the two came to town after they had plotted our destruction. Telemachus came first, and then after him came Odysseus, accompanied by the swineherd, dressed in rags and leaning on a staff like some miserable old beggar. He came so unexpectedly that none of us recognized him, not even the older ones among us, and we insulted him and threw things at him. He endured both the blows and the insults without a word, though he was in his own house. But when the will of Zeus who bears the aegis inspired him, he and Telemachus took the weapons and hid them in an inner room, bolting the doors behind them. Then he cleverly had his wife offer his bow and a quantity of iron axes to be competed for by us ill-fated suitors, and this was the beginning of our end, for not one of us could string the bow—we couldn't even come close. When it was about to reach Odysseus's hands, we all shouted that it should not be given to him, no matter what he said, but Telemachus insisted on his having it. When he got it in his hands he strung it easily and sent his arrow through the iron. Then he stood on the floor of the hall and poured his arrows on the ground, glaring fiercely around him. First he killed Antinous, and then, aiming straight ahead, he let fly his deadly arrows and they fell thick upon us. It was clear that one of the gods was helping them, for they attacked us with overwhelming force throughout the halls, and there was a hideous sound of groaning as our heads were smashed in, and the ground ran with our blood. This, Agamemnon, is how we met our end, and our bodies are still lying uncared for in Odysseus's house, for our friends at home do not yet know what has happened, so they cannot lay us out and wash the black blood from our wounds, mourning over us according to the rites due to the dead."

"Fortunate Odysseus, son of Laertes," replied Agamemnon's spirit, "you are indeed blessed in having a wife endowed with such excellent understanding and so faithful to her wedded husband as Penelope, daughter of Icarius. The fame of her virtue shall never die, and the immortals shall compose a song that will be welcome to all mankind in honor of Penelope's faithfulness. How different was the wickedness of Tyndareus's daughter, who killed her lawful husband. Her song shall be hateful among men, for she has brought disgrace upon all womankind, even the good ones."

So they talked in the house of Hades deep within the bowels of the earth. Meanwhile Odysseus and the others left the town and soon reached the beautiful, well-tended farm of Laertes, which he had claimed through endless labor. Here was his house, with a lean-to running all around it where the slaves who worked for him slept and sat and ate, while inside the house there was an old Sicilian woman who looked after him on this country farm. When Odysseus arrived, he said to his son and the other two:
"Go to the house and kill the best pig you can find for dinner. Meanwhile I want to see whether my father will recognize me or fail to know me after such a long absence."

He then took off his armor and gave it to Eumaeus and Philoetius, who went straight to the house, while he turned toward the vineyard to test his father. As he went down into the great orchard, he did not see Dolius or any of his sons or the other servants, for they were all gathering thorns to make a fence for the vineyard at the place where the old man had told them. So he found his father alone, hoeing around a vine. He wore a dirty old shirt, patched and very shabby. His legs were bound with leather straps to protect him from thorns, and he also wore leather sleeves. He had a goatskin cap on his head and looked very sorrowful. When Odysseus saw him so worn out, so old and full of grief, he stood still under a tall pear tree and began to weep. He wondered whether to embrace him, kiss him, and tell him all about his homecoming, or whether he should first question him and see what he would say. In the end he decided it would be best to test him with words, so with this in mind he approached his father, who was bending down and working around a plant.

"I see, sir," said Odysseus, "that you are an excellent gardener—what care you take with everything. There is not a single plant, fig tree, vine, olive, pear, or flower bed that doesn't show the trace of your attention. I hope you won't be offended if I say that you take better care of your garden than of yourself. You are old, unkempt, and very poorly dressed. It can't be because you're lazy that your master takes such poor care of you. Indeed, your face and figure have nothing of the slave about them and show you to be of noble birth. I would have said you were one of those who should wash well, eat well, and sleep comfortably at night, as old men have a right to do. But tell me, and tell me truthfully, whose servant are you, and in whose garden are you working? Tell me also about another matter. Is this place I've come to really Ithaca? I met a man just now who said so, but he was a dull fellow and didn't have the patience to hear my story when I was asking him about an old friend of mine, whether he was still living or already dead and in Hades' house. Believe me when I tell you that this man once came to my house when I was in my own country, and never did any stranger come to me whom I liked better. He said his family was from Ithaca and that his father was Laertes, son of Arcesius. I received him hospitably, welcoming him to all the abundance of my house, and when he left I gave him all the customary gifts. I gave him seven talents of fine gold and a cup of solid silver with flowers engraved on it. I gave him twelve light cloaks and as many pieces of tapestry. I also gave him twelve single-fold cloaks, twelve rugs, twelve fine mantles, and an equal number of shirts. To all this I added four beautiful women skilled in all useful arts, and I let him choose which ones he wanted."

His father shed tears and answered, "Sir, you have indeed come to the country you named, but it has fallen into the hands of wicked people. All this wealth of gifts has been given for nothing. If you could have found your friend here alive in Ithaca, he would have entertained you hospitably and repaid your gifts amply when you left him—as would have been only right considering what you had already given him. But tell me truthfully, how many years has it been since you entertained this guest—my unhappy son, if he ever existed? Alas! He has died far from his own country. The fish of the sea have eaten him, or he has fallen prey to the birds and wild beasts of some land. Neither his mother nor I, his father, who gave him life, could wrap our arms around him and shroud him, nor could his excellent and richly dowered wife Penelope mourn her husband as was proper at his deathbed and close his eyes according to the rites due to the dead. But now tell me truthfully, for I want to know: Who are you and where do you come from? Tell me of your city and parents. Where is the ship that brought you and your men to Ithaca? Or were you a passenger on someone else's ship, and those who brought you here have gone on their way and left you?"

"I will tell you everything quite truthfully," answered Odysseus. "I come from Alybas, where I have a fine house. I am the son of King Apheidas, who is the son of Polypemon. My own name is Eperitus. Heaven drove me off course as I was leaving Sicily, and I have been brought here against my will. My ship is lying over there, off the open country outside the town, and this is the fifth year since Odysseus left my country. Poor fellow, yet the omens were good for him when he left me. The birds all flew on our right hands, and both he and I rejoiced to see them as we parted, for we had every hope that we would have another friendly meeting and exchange gifts."

A dark cloud of sorrow fell upon Laertes as he listened. He filled both hands with dust from the ground and poured it over his gray head, groaning heavily as he did so. Odysseus's heart was touched, and his nostrils quivered as he looked at his father. Then he sprang toward him, threw his arms around him and kissed him, saying, "I am he, father, the one you're asking about—I have returned after being away for twenty years. But stop your sighing and weeping—we have no time to lose, for I should tell you that I have been killing the suitors in my house, to punish them for their arrogance and crimes."
"If you really are my son Odysseus," replied Laertes, "and have come back again, you must give me clear proof of your identity that will convince me."

"First look at this scar," answered Odysseus, "which I got from a boar's tusk when I was hunting on Mount Parnassus. You and my mother had sent me to Autolycus, my mother's father, to receive the gifts he had promised to give me when he was here. Furthermore, I will point out to you the trees in the vineyard that you gave me, and I asked you about them all as I followed you around the garden. We went over them all, and you told me their names and what they all were. You gave me thirteen pear trees, ten apple trees, and forty fig trees. You also said you would give me fifty rows of vines with corn planted between each row, and they yield grapes of every kind when heaven's heat has been laid heavy upon them."

Laertes's strength failed him when he heard the convincing proofs his son had given him. He threw his arms around him, and Odysseus had to support him or he would have fainted. But as soon as he recovered and was beginning to regain his senses, he said, "O father Zeus, then you gods are still on Olympus after all, if the suitors have really been punished for their arrogance and folly. Nevertheless, I am very afraid that I shall have all the townspeople of Ithaca up here soon, and they will be sending messengers everywhere throughout the cities of the Cephallenians."

Odysseus answered, "Take heart and don't worry about that, but let's go into the house near your garden. I have already told Telemachus, Philoetius, and Eumaeus to go there and get dinner ready as quickly as possible."

So the two made their way toward the house talking together. When they arrived they found Telemachus with the cattle herder and the swineherd cutting up meat and mixing wine with water. Then the old Sicilian woman took Laertes inside and washed him and anointed him with oil. She put a good cloak on him, and Athena came to him and gave him a more impressive appearance, making him taller and stronger than before. When he came back, his son was amazed to see him looking so godlike and said to him, "My dear father, one of the gods has been making you much taller and better-looking."

Laertes answered, "Would that by Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo I were the man I was when I ruled among the Cephallenians and took Nericum, that strong fortress on the headland. If I were still what I was then and had been in our house yesterday with my armor on, I would have been able to stand by you and help you against the suitors. I would have killed a great many of them, and you would have rejoiced to see it."

So they talked, but the others, when they had finished their work and the feast was ready, stopped working and took their proper places on the benches and seats. Then they began eating. Soon old Dolius and his sons left their work and came up, for their mother, the Sicilian woman who looked after Laertes now that he was growing old, had gone to fetch them. When they saw Odysseus and were certain it was he, they stood there lost in amazement. But Odysseus scolded them good-naturedly and said, "Sit down to your dinner, old man, and don't worry about your surprise. We have been wanting to begin for some time and have been waiting for you."

Then Dolius stretched out both his hands and went up to Odysseus. "Sir," he said, seizing his master's hand and kissing it at the wrist, "we have long been wishing for your return, and now heaven has restored you to us after we had given up hope. All hail, and may the gods bless you. But tell me, does Penelope already know of your return, or should we send someone to tell her?"

"Old man," answered Odysseus, "she already knows, so you don't need to worry about that." With this he took his seat, and Dolius's sons gathered around Odysseus to greet him and embrace him one after another. Then they took their seats in proper order near their father Dolius.

While they were busy preparing their dinner, Rumor went around the town and spread news of the terrible fate that had befallen the suitors. As soon as the people heard of it, they gathered from every quarter, groaning and wailing before Odysseus's house. They took away the dead, buried each man his own, and put the bodies of those from elsewhere on board fishing boats for the fishermen to take each to his own place. Then they met angrily in the assembly place, and when they were gathered together, Eupeithes rose to speak. He was overwhelmed with grief for the death of his son Antinous, who had been the first man killed by Odysseus, so he said, weeping bitterly, "My friends, this man has done the Greeks great wrong. He took many of our best men away with him in his fleet, and he lost both ships and men. Now, moreover, on his return he has been killing all the leading men among the Cephallenians. Let's act before he can get away to Pylos or to Elis where the Epeans rule, or we shall be ashamed of ourselves forever. It will be an everlasting disgrace to us if we do not avenge the murder of our sons and brothers. For my own part, I would have no more pleasure in life but would rather die at once. Let's go after them before they can cross over to the mainland."

He wept as he spoke, and everyone pitied him. But Medon and the bard Phemius had now awakened and came to them from Odysseus's house. Everyone was astonished to see them, but they stood in the middle of the assembly, and Medon said, "Hear me, men of Ithaca. Odysseus did not do these things against the will of heaven. I myself saw an immortal god take the form of Mentor and stand beside him. This god appeared, now in front of him encouraging him, and now going furiously about the hall and attacking the suitors, and they fell thick upon one another."
At this, pale fear seized them, and old Halitherses, son of Mastor, rose to speak, for he was the only man among them who knew both past and future. So he spoke to them plainly and honestly, saying,

"Men of Ithaca, it is all your own fault that things have turned out as they have. You would not listen to me or to Mentor when we told you to check the folly of your sons, who were doing much wrong in the recklessness of their hearts—wasting the wealth and dishonoring the wife of a chief who they thought would never return. Now, however, let it be as I say, and do as I tell you. Do not go out against Odysseus, or you may find that you have been bringing evil upon your own heads."

This was what he said, and more than half raised a loud shout and immediately left the assembly. But the rest stayed where they were, for Halitherses's speech displeased them, and they sided with Eupeithes. They therefore hurried off for their weapons, and when they had armed themselves, they met together in front of the city, and Eupeithes led them on in their folly. He thought he was going to avenge his son's murder, but in truth he would never return home and was himself destined to die in the attempt.
Then Athena said to Zeus, "Father, son of Cronus, king of kings, answer me this question—What do you intend to do? Will you make them fight still more, or will you make peace between them?"

And Zeus answered, "My child, why do you ask me? Wasn't it your own plan that Odysseus should come home and take his revenge on the suitors? Do whatever you like, but I will tell you what I think would be the most reasonable arrangement. Now that Odysseus has had his revenge, let them swear to a solemn covenant by which he shall continue to rule, while we cause the others to forgive and forget the massacre of their sons and brothers. Let them all become friends as before, and let peace and prosperity reign."
This was what Athena was already eager to bring about, so down she darted from the highest peaks of Olympus.

Now when Laertes and the others had finished dinner, Odysseus began by saying, "Some of you go out and see if they are getting close to us." So one of Dolius's sons went as he was told. Standing on the threshold, he could see them all quite near and said to Odysseus, "Here they are. Let's put on our armor at once."

They armed themselves as quickly as they could—that is, Odysseus, his three men, and Dolius's six sons. Laertes and Dolius did the same—warriors by necessity despite their gray hair. When they had all put on their armor, they opened the gate and marched out, with Odysseus leading the way.

Then Zeus's daughter Athena came up to them, having taken the form and voice of Mentor. Odysseus was glad when he saw her and said to his son Telemachus, "Telemachus, now that you are about to fight in a battle that will show every man's courage, be sure not to disgrace your ancestors, who were famous for their strength and bravery throughout the world."
"You speak truly, my dear father," answered Telemachus, "and you shall see, if you wish, that I have no intention of disgracing your family."
Laertes was delighted when he heard this. "Good heavens," he exclaimed, "what a day I am having! I do indeed rejoice at it. My son and grandson are competing with each other in courage."
At this Athena came close to him and said, "Son of Arcesius—dearest of all my friends—pray to the gray-eyed maiden and to Zeus her father, then aim your spear and throw it."

As she spoke, she filled him with fresh strength, and when he had prayed to her, he aimed his spear and hurled it. He struck Eupeithes's helmet, and the spear went right through it, for the helmet could not stop it, and his armor rang as he fell heavily to the ground. Meanwhile Odysseus and his son attacked the front line of the enemy and struck them down with their swords and spears. Indeed, they would have killed every one of them and prevented them from ever getting home again, but Athena raised her voice loud and made everyone stop. "Men of Ithaca," she cried, "cease this dreadful war and settle the matter at once without further bloodshed."

At this, pale fear seized everyone. They were so frightened that their weapons dropped from their hands and fell to the ground at the sound of the goddess's voice, and they fled back to the city to save their lives. But Odysseus gave a great cry and, gathering himself together, swooped down like a soaring eagle. Then the son of Cronus sent a thunderbolt that fell just in front of Athena, so she said to Odysseus, "Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, stop this warlike strife, or Zeus will be angry with you."
So spoke Athena, and Odysseus obeyed her gladly. Then Athena, in the form and voice of Mentor, made a covenant of peace between the two opposing sides.
